video.title: How I Built This $160K/Month Gym App

summary: Starter Story's Pat Walls interviews Mauro, a 22-23-year-old founder of Symmetry, a gym tracking app localised for Spain and Mexico that reports about $160k monthly revenue and about $3 million total after one year. Growth came from UGC rather than their YouTube audience or influencers: nearly 80,000 videos across 500+ accounts, almost a billion views, with nearly half of revenue paid to creators. The core of the interview is his product method: set ambitious quarterly OKRs, instrument every onboarding screen, use interviews for the 'why', start from problems, and A/B test everything for at least two weeks with guardrail metrics. A single commitment screen added 3% retention while redesigns of the home screen moved nothing. Key takeaway: localise into an underserved market and let experiments, not instinct, decide what to build.

ideas.name: Localised gym tracking app for the Spanish-speaking market (Symmetry)
ideas.one_liner: A gym workout tracker with ranks, streaks and a social feed, localised for Spain and Mexico, grown with UGC to about $160k a month in one year.
ideas.business_model: Consumer app subscriptions via App Store and Google Play paywall
ideas.customer: Gym-goers in Spanish-speaking markets (mainly Spain and Mexico), including beginners
ideas.problem: Tracking workouts, weights and reps; staying motivated to train
ideas.offer: Workout plans, set/rep/weight tracking, exercise videos, per-muscle and per-exercise ranks, streaks, social feed of friends' workouts

pricing.model: Subscription behind a paywall (prices not stated)
pricing.notes: Paywall is A/B tested with Superwall; about half of revenue goes to UGC creators.

acquisition_channels.details: UGC network: nearly 80,000 short videos in a year across 500+ accounts, nearly a billion views; formats segmented and tracked (e.g. iPhone lock-screen notification format; one video hit 17 million views). Creators paid nearly half of revenue.

quote.text: In the last year we have posted nearly 80,000 videos. We have more than 500 accounts
quote.speaker: Mauro

acquisition_channels.details: Founders' prior fitness YouTube channel gave a small launch spike but was not a scalable channel.

quote.text: we had this YouTube community that we thought it was going to be really good for growing the app. It wasn't
quote.speaker: Mauro

acquisition_channels.details: Influencer marketing was tried and did not work.
Distributed on iOS and Android app stores.

ideas.delivery: Small founding team (former fitness YouTubers) builds and iterates the app using quarterly OKRs, event analytics, user interviews and A/B tests of at least two weeks.
unit_economics_claims: About $3 million total revenue across iOS and Android
Nearly half of revenue paid to creators
One onboarding commitment screen increased retention by 3%
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Launched about a year ago; company started two years ago

acquisition.how: UGC video production and posting can be heavily templated and partly AI-assisted, but they rely on 500+ accounts run with paid human creators.

delivery.how: Software app; content and features maintained by the team.

support.how: In-app and community support; some human input.

uk_applicability.notes: Consumer fitness apps work the same in the UK; localisation to an underserved language/region is the key lesson. UK GDPR applies to health/fitness data; mass multi-account posting may breach platform rules.

risks: UGC economics depend on revenue per download; paying ~50% of revenue to creators squeezes margin
Running 500+ social accounts risks platform bans

tactics.name: UGC format factory
steps: Run hundreds of social accounts posting short videos
Segment every video into formats and sub-formats and track performance
Double down on winners, e.g. fake iPhone lock-screen notifications ending with an app notification to go to the gym
Pay creators a large revenue share (about half) so they keep producing long term
Use average revenue per download (varies by country) to set what you can pay creators

quote.text: we segment the videos into formats
quote.speaker: Mauro

tactics.name: Experiment policy for product decisions
steps: Set ambitious quarterly OKRs (more ambitious when the app is new) and review metrics weekly or daily
Find high-leverage screens (paywall, onboarding, search) instead of cosmetic features
Track every onboarding screen with analytics for the 'what'
Interview users and read Discord/Reddit for the 'why'
Start from a validated problem, write hypotheses with expected metric impact and guardrail metrics
A/B test against control for at least two weeks, then analyse; log all tests in a database

quote.text: after at least two weeks of running the experiment, you then analyze the data
quote.speaker: Mauro

tactics.name: Pick the right activation metric
steps: Define activation for your product (for a gym app: going to the gym and tracking a workout)
Treat activation as the lead indicator for retention
Track first-week and 30-day retention and revenue per download

quote.text: if you move activation for attention, follows
quote.speaker: Mauro

warnings.warning: Building what you want, or literally what users request, gives terrible to mediocre results.

quote.text: First we built what we wanted, terrible idea. Second, we built what users wanted
quote.speaker: Mauro

warnings.warning: The most common mistake is having no analytics events at all, so you cannot see where users drop off.

quote.text: the most common error I see everybody is not tracking anything like they don't have any events at all in their app
quote.speaker: Mauro

warnings.warning: An existing YouTube audience and influencer marketing did not produce scalable growth.
Most tests move nothing; completely different redesigns of the home screen had zero metric impact.

quote.text: they moved nothing to the matrix. Absolutely nothing. And they were completely different designs
quote.speaker: Mauro

lessons.lesson: Localising a proven app category for an underserved language market can win even in a saturated category.
Focus on high-leverage screens like the paywall, onboarding and search; cosmetic features affect few users.
Use analytics for where users drop off and conversations for why.

quote.text: For the why, you need qualitative data
quote.speaker: Mauro

lessons.lesson: Come from the problem space, not the solution space, before designing experiments.

quote.text: you're not coming from a solution place. You must come from a problem space
quote.speaker: Mauro

lessons.lesson: Revenue per download decides how much you can pay for acquisition, and it varies a lot by country.
Paying creators generously keeps them producing content long term.
Most changes do not move metrics; knowing this pushes you to focus more on marketing than product.

quote.text: So most things don't make a difference
quote.speaker: Pat Walls

lessons.lesson: Play long-term games with long-term people; the company started a year before launch and they were bad at first.

quote.text: I would say to play long-term games with long-term people
quote.speaker: Mauro
